role: TCA cycle intermediate that links carbon and nitrogen metabolism through transamination.
Main circulating ketone body. The mammary gland uses it for fat synthesis; raised levels point to negative energy balance.
Short-chain fatty acid from rumen fermentation and the main carbon source for de novo milk fat synthesis.
Ketone body produced by the liver when body fat is mobilised, typically in early lactation.
Ketone body formed from acetoacetate; milk acetone is used when screening herds for ketosis.
Glucogenic amino acid taken up from blood; also a building block of milk proteins.
Amino acid that links the TCA cycle with nitrogen metabolism.
Methyl donor formed by oxidising choline; also an osmolyte found in some feeds such as beet.
Short-chain fatty acid; free butyrate in milk can come from rumen-derived precursors and from lipolysis of milk fat.
Medium-chain fatty acids made de novo in the mammary gland; free forms rise when milk fat is broken down.
Carries long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria so they can be oxidised for energy.
Essential nutrient and precursor of phosphatidylcholine; milk carries it mostly as phosphocholine and glycerophosphocholine.
Major organic acid of milk, made in the mammary gland and tied to de novo fat synthesis; proposed as an energy-balance indicator.
TCA cycle intermediate between citrate and isocitrate.
Energy buffer: it stores high-energy phosphate as creatine phosphate.
High-energy phosphate store that regenerates ATP quickly.
Breakdown product of creatine phosphate that reflects muscle turnover.
Sulfur compound from feed and microbial metabolism; its milk level is often linked to diet.
Amine produced when microbes break down choline and related compounds.
Head group of phosphatidylethanolamine, a membrane phospholipid.
One-carbon unit produced during rumen fermentation.
Deoxy sugar found in milk oligosaccharides and glycoproteins.
TCA cycle intermediate.
Monosaccharide that forms half of each lactose molecule.
Lactose precursor; in ruminants it comes mostly from liver gluconeogenesis.
Intermediate on the route from glucose to UDP-galactose and lactose.
One of the most abundant free amino acids in milk.
Glycine conjugate of benzoic acid derived from plant phenolics, so it tends to be higher on fresh forage.
Branched-chain fatty acid formed when rumen microbes ferment valine.
Branched-chain essential amino acid.
End product of anaerobic glycolysis; bacterial activity in milk can also raise it.
Main milk sugar; it draws water into milk and so largely sets milk volume.
Branched-chain essential amino acid and a signal for protein synthesis.
TCA cycle intermediate.
Dicarboxylic acid related to malonyl-CoA, the building block of fatty acid synthesis.
Released when microbes degrade pectin in forage.
Amino sugar of milk oligosaccharides and glycoproteins; tends to be higher in early-lactation milk.
Acetyl ester of carnitine that reflects fatty acid oxidation and acetyl-CoA turnover.
One of the main forms in which milk carries choline.
Precursor of pyrimidine nucleotides and characteristically abundant in ruminant milk.
Aromatic essential amino acid and precursor of tyrosine.
Amino acid that is especially abundant in casein.
Short-chain fatty acid from the rumen and the main glucose precursor in ruminants.
End product of glycolysis and entry point to the TCA cycle.
TCA cycle intermediate that is also produced by rumen microbes.
Microbial product of choline breakdown; at high levels it gives milk a fishy taint.
Aromatic amino acid formed from phenylalanine.
End product of protein metabolism; milk urea is used to judge how well dietary protein is used.
Pyrimidine nucleoside involved in nucleotide and sugar-nucleotide metabolism.
Short-chain fatty acid from rumen fermentation.
Branched-chain essential amino acid.
Choline-containing breakdown product of phosphatidylcholine and a major choline form in milk.
